The Great Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Fascicle 585. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang under Imperial Decree. Part Three of the Twelfth Section on the Pāramitā of Pure Ethics. "What is called skillfulness regarding dependent origination?"

It refers to bodhisattvas who, as it truly is, understand the various specific characteristics of all causal conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*), and who, as it truly is, understand the various specific characteristics of all immediately preceding conditions (*samanantara-pratyaya*), objective conditions (*ālambana-pratyaya*), dominant conditions (*adhipati-pratyaya*), and all phenomena produced from these conditions; this is called skillfulness regarding dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda-kauśalya*).

Furthermore, when Bodhisattvas correctly understand that the various specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) of all causes and conditions are unapprehendable, and correctly understand that the various specific characteristics of all equal-and-immediate conditions (*samanantarapratyaya*), objective conditions (*ālambanapratyaya*), predominant conditions (*adhipatipratyaya*), and all phenomena produced from these conditions are likewise unapprehendable—this is called skillfulness regarding dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpādakauśalya*).

Furthermore, when Bodhisattvas accurately understand the various common characteristics of all causal conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*), and accurately understand the various common characteristics of all immediately preceding conditions (*samanantara-pratyaya*), objective conditions (*ālambana-pratyaya*), dominant conditions (*adhipati-pratyaya*), and all phenomena produced from these conditions, this is called skillfulness regarding dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda-kauśalya*).

Furthermore, when Bodhisattvas correctly understand that the various common characteristics of all causal conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*) are unapprehendable, and correctly understand that the various common characteristics of all equal-and-immediate conditions (*samanantara-pratyaya*), objective conditions (*ālambana-pratyaya*), and dominant conditions (*adhipati-pratyaya*), as well as the phenomena produced from these conditions, are all unapprehendable—this is called skillfulness regarding dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda-kauśalya*).

Furthermore, when Bodhisattvas understand as it truly is that all causes and conditions—whether permanent or impermanent—are unfindable, and when they understand as it truly is that all equal-and-immediate conditions, object conditions, predominant conditions, and all phenomena produced from these conditions—whether permanent or impermanent—are unfindable, this is called skillfulness regarding dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda-kauśalya*).

Furthermore, when Bodhisattvas understand, as it truly is, that all causes and conditions—whether pleasure or pain—are unapprehendable; and when they understand, as it truly is, that all equal-and-immediate conditions, objective conditions, dominant conditions, and all phenomena produced from these conditions—whether pleasure or pain—are likewise unapprehendable; this is called skill in dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda-kauśalya*).

Furthermore, when bodhisattvas understand as it truly is that all causes and conditions—whether characterized by a self or devoid of a self—are unapprehendable; and when they understand as it truly is that all immediately preceding conditions, objective conditions, dominant conditions, and the phenomena arising from these conditions—whether characterized by a self or devoid of a self—are unapprehendable, this is called skillfulness regarding dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda-kauśalya*).

Furthermore, when Bodhisattvas understand as it truly is that all causes and conditions—whether pure or impure—are unapprehendable; and when they understand as it truly is that all equal-and-immediate conditions, objective conditions, dominant conditions, and all phenomena produced from these conditions—whether pure or impure—are likewise unapprehendable; this is called skillfulness regarding dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda-kauśalya*).

Furthermore, when Bodhisattvas understand as they truly are that all causal conditions—whether empty or non-empty—are unapprehendable; and when they understand as they truly are that all immediate conditions, objective conditions, dominant conditions, and all phenomena produced from these conditions—whether empty or non-empty—are likewise unapprehendable; this is called skillfulness regarding dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda-kauśalya*).

Furthermore, when bodhisattvas correctly understand that all causal conditions—whether characterized by signs or signless—are unapprehendable, and when they correctly understand that all immediately preceding conditions, objective conditions, dominant conditions, and all phenomena produced from these conditions—whether characterized by signs or signless—are likewise unapprehendable, this is called skillfulness regarding dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda-kauśalya*).

Furthermore, bodhisattvas understand as it truly is that all causal conditions—whether they involve aspiration or lack aspiration—are unfindable; they understand as it truly is that all immediate conditions, objective conditions, dominant conditions, and all phenomena produced from these conditions—whether they involve aspiration or lack aspiration—are unfindable. This is called skillfulness regarding dependent origination.

Furthermore, when Bodhisattvas correctly understand that all causes and conditions—whether quiescent or non-quiescent—are unapprehendable, and correctly understand that all equal-and-immediate conditions, objective conditions, dominant conditions, and all phenomena produced from these conditions—whether quiescent or non-quiescent—are likewise unapprehendable, this is called skillfulness regarding dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda-kauśalya*).

Furthermore, bodhisattvas understand as it truly is that all causes and conditions—whether they are separated from or not separated from [their effects]—are unapprehendable; they understand as it truly is that all immediately preceding conditions (*samanantara-pratyaya*), objective conditions (*ālambana-pratyaya*), dominant conditions (*adhipati-pratyaya*), and all phenomena produced from these conditions—whether they are separated from or not separated from [their conditions]—are unapprehendable. This is called skillfulness regarding dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda-kauśalya*).

Furthermore, when Bodhisattvas accurately understand the various specific characteristics of all ignorance, and accurately understand the various specific characteristics of all volitional formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, grasping, becoming, birth, and aging-and-death—this is called skillfulness regarding dependent origination.

Furthermore, when Bodhisattvas correctly understand that the various specific characteristics of all ignorance are unapprehendable, and correctly understand that the various specific characteristics of all formative forces, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, grasping, becoming, birth, and old age and death are unapprehendable—this is called skillfulness regarding dependent origination.

Furthermore, when bodhisattvas accurately understand the various common characteristics of all ignorance, and accurately understand the various common characteristics of all volitional formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, grasping, becoming, birth, and aging-and-death, this is called skillfulness regarding dependent origination.

Furthermore, when bodhisattvas, in accordance with reality, understand that all the various common characteristics of ignorance are unapprehendable, and likewise understand that all the various common characteristics of volitional formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, grasping, becoming, birth, and old age and death are unapprehendable—this is called skillfulness regarding dependent origination.

Furthermore, when bodhisattvas correctly understand that all ignorance—whether permanent or impermanent—is unapprehendable, and correctly understand that all formative factors (*saṃskāra*), consciousness (*vijñāna*), name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*), contact (*sparśa*), sensation (*vedanā*), craving (*tṭṛṣṇā*), grasping (*upādāna*), becoming (*bhava*), birth (*jāti*), and old age and death (*jarāmaraṇa*)—whether permanent or impermanent—are unapprehendable, this is called skill in dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda-kauśalya*).

Furthermore, when Bodhisattvas correctly understand that all ignorance—whether pleasure or pain—is unapprehendable, and correctly understand that all formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, grasping, becoming, birth, and old age and death—whether pleasure or pain—are unapprehendable, this is called skillfulness regarding dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda-kauśalya*).

Furthermore, bodhisattvas correctly understand that all ignorance—whether as self or as non-self—is unapprehendable; they correctly understand that all formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, grasping, becoming, birth, and aging-and-death—whether as self or as non-self—are unapprehendable. This is called skillfulness regarding dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda-kauśalya*).

Furthermore, when Bodhisattvas, in accordance with reality, understand that all ignorance—whether pure or impure—is unapprehendable, and when they, in accordance with reality, understand that all formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, sensation, craving, grasping, becoming, birth, and old age and death—whether pure or impure—are unapprehendable, this is called skillfulness regarding dependent origination.

Furthermore, when bodhisattvas correctly understand that all ignorance—whether empty or non-empty—is unapprehendable, and correctly understand that all formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, grasping, becoming, birth, and old age and death—whether empty or non-empty—are unapprehendable, this is called skillfulness regarding dependent origination.

Furthermore, bodhisattvas understand as it truly is that all ignorance—whether characterized by signs or signless—is unapprehendable; they understand as it truly is that all formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, grasping, becoming, birth, and aging-and-death—whether characterized by signs or signless—are unapprehendable. This is called skillfulness regarding dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda-kauśalya*).

Furthermore, bodhisattvas understand as it truly is that all ignorance—whether with aspiration or without aspiration—is unapprehendable; they understand as it truly is that all formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, grasping, becoming, birth, and old age and death—whether with aspiration or without aspiration—are unapprehendable. This is called skillfulness regarding dependent origination.

Furthermore, when bodhisattvas understand as it truly is that all ignorance—whether quiescent or non-quiescent—is unapprehendable, and when they understand as it truly is that all formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, grasping, becoming, birth, and aging-and-death—whether quiescent or non-quiescent—are unapprehendable, this is called skillfulness regarding dependent origination.

Furthermore, bodhisattvas understand as it truly is that all ignorance—whether it is separated from or not separated from [the other members]—is unfindable; they understand as it truly is that all formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, grasping, becoming, birth, and aging-and-death—whether they are separated from or not separated from [ignorance]—are unfindable. This is called skill in dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda-kauśalya*).
"What is meant by skillfulness regarding what is possible and what is impossible?

It refers to a bodhisattva’s accurate understanding of the various specific characteristics of all that is possible, and their accurate understanding of the various specific characteristics of all that is impossible; this is called skillfulness regarding what is possible and what is impossible."

Furthermore, when bodhisattvas accurately understand that the various specific characteristics of all possible bases (*sthāna*) are ultimately unapprehendable, and accurately understand that the various specific characteristics of all impossible bases (*asthāna*) are likewise unapprehendable, this is called skillfulness regarding the possible and the impossible (*sthānāsthāna-kauśalya*).

Furthermore, when bodhisattvas accurately understand the various common characteristics of all that is possible (*sthāna*), and accurately understand the various common characteristics of all that is impossible (*asthāna*), this is called skillfulness regarding what is possible and what is impossible.

Furthermore, when bodhisattvas truly understand that the various common characteristics of all possible bases (*sthāna*) are unapprehendable, and truly understand that the various common characteristics of all impossible bases (*asthāna*) are unapprehendable, this is called skill in the possible and the impossible (*sthānāsthānakauśalya*).

Furthermore, when Bodhisattvas understand as it truly is that in all instances (sthāna) whether permanent or impermanent, nothing can be apprehended, and understand as it truly is that in all non-instances (asthāna) whether permanent or impermanent, nothing can be apprehended—this is called skill in what is possible and what is impossible (sthānāsthāna-kauśalya).

Furthermore, bodhisattvas understand as it truly is that in all possible cases (sthāna), whether pleasure or pain, neither can be apprehended; they understand as it truly is that in all impossible cases (asthāna), whether pleasure or pain, neither can be apprehended. This is called skill in what is possible and what is impossible (sthānāsthāna-kauśalya).

Furthermore, bodhisattvas know as it truly is that in all instances where there is a self or no-self, neither can be apprehended; they know as it truly is that in all instances where there is not [an instance], neither a self nor no-self can be apprehended. This is called skillfulness regarding what is possible and what is impossible (*sthānāsthāna-kauśalya*).

Furthermore, when Bodhisattvas understand as it truly is that all possible bases (*sthāna*), whether pure or impure, are unapprehendable, and understand as it truly is that all impossible bases (*asthāna*), whether pure or impure, are likewise unapprehendable—this is called skill in the possible and the impossible (*sthānāsthāna-kauśalya*).

Furthermore, bodhisattvas understand as it truly is that all possible cases (*sthāna*), whether empty or not empty, are unapprehendable; they understand as it truly is that all impossible cases (*asthāna*), whether empty or not empty, are unapprehendable. This is called skillfulness regarding the possible and the impossible (*sthānāsthāna-kauśalya*).

Furthermore, bodhisattvas accurately understand that in all instances (*sthāna*), whether characterized by signs (*sanimitta*) or signless (*animitta*), nothing can be apprehended; they accurately understand that in all non-instances (*asthāna*), whether characterized by signs or signless, nothing can be apprehended. This is called skillfulness regarding what is possible and what is impossible (*sthānāsthāna-kauśalya*).

Furthermore, bodhisattvas understand as it truly is that in all instances (sthāna), whether there is an aspiration or no aspiration, neither can be apprehended; they understand as it truly is that in all non-instances (asthāna), whether there is an aspiration or no aspiration, neither can be apprehended. This is called skillfulness regarding what is possible and what is impossible (sthānāsthāna-kauśalya).

Furthermore, when Bodhisattvas truly understand that all possible bases (*sthāna*), whether peaceful or not peaceful, are unapprehendable, and truly understand that all impossible bases (*asthāna*), whether peaceful or not peaceful, are likewise unapprehendable—this is called skill in the possible and the impossible (*sthānāsthānakauśalya*).

Furthermore, bodhisattvas understand as they truly are that in all instances (*sthāna*), whether involving detachment or non-detachment, nothing can be apprehended; they understand as they truly are that in all non-instances (*asthāna*), whether involving detachment or non-detachment, nothing can be apprehended. This is called skill in *sthāna* and *asthāna*.

"In this way, a bodhisattva should cultivate skillfulness regarding the aggregates and so forth; by means of such skillfulness, they teach the Dharma to sentient beings as appropriate, causing them to permanently sever and extinguish the perception of a 'sentient being' and other such notions."

When a bodhisattva thus gives rise to such a sublime mind and cultivates all manner of wondrous wisdom for the benefit of both self and others—making great compassion the foremost of all—and is constantly able to generate a mind that accords with the wisdom of omniscience through its corresponding dedication, one should know that this is called a bodhisattva endowed with ethical discipline; it should be known that they are fully possessed of unsurpassed pure precepts.

If bodhisattvas wish to seek unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, they should diligently cultivate the perfections of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom, dedicating these toward the pursuit of the knowledge of all modes.

If bodhisattvas dedicate these six perfections toward the pursuit of the knowledge of all modes, then by means of this pure ethical discipline, those bodhisattvas universally surpass all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
"Furthermore, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra!

The single precept of a bodhisattva who has first resolved to attain unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment surpasses the ten paths of wholesome action accomplished by all sentient beings a hundredfold, a thousandfold, and even up to an *upaniṣad*-fold."
"Furthermore, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra!
Suppose all sentient beings in the world were to fully accomplish the ten paths of wholesome action;

the precepts possessed by them would not equal even one hundredth part, nor one thousandth part, nor even an *upaniṣad* part of the single bodhisattva precept of a bodhisattva who has first resolved upon unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."
"Furthermore, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra!
Suppose all sentient beings in the world were to fully accomplish the first five supernormal powers;

the aggregate of their precepts would not equal even one hundredth part, nor one thousandth part, nor even an *upaniṣad* part of a single bodhisattva precept taken by a bodhisattva at the moment of first generating the mind set on unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."
"Furthermore, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra!
Suppose all sentient beings in the world were to fully abide in loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity;

the precepts possessed by them would not equal even one hundredth part, nor one thousandth part, nor even an *upaniṣad* part of a single bodhisattva precept of those bodhisattvas who have first resolved their minds toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening."
"Furthermore, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra!
Suppose all sentient beings in the world were to fully accomplish the patience that accords with emptiness;

the precepts they possess would not equal even one hundredth part, nor one thousandth part, nor even an *upaniṣad* fraction of the precept of a single bodhisattva at the time of their first resolve among those bodhisattvas who have generated the mind of unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment."
“Furthermore, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra!
Suppose all sentient beings in the world were to fully accomplish the patience that accords with the signless;

their collective precepts would not equal one hundredth part, nor one thousandth part, nor even one *upaniṣad* part of a single bodhisattva precept taken by a bodhisattva at the initial moment of generating the mind set on unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.”
"Furthermore, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra!
Suppose all sentient beings in the world were to fully accomplish the patience that accords with wishlessness;

their collective precepts would not equal even one-hundredth part, nor one-thousandth part, nor even an *upaniṣad* fraction of a single bodhisattva precept taken at the initial moment of generating the mind set on unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening by those bodhisattvas."
"Furthermore, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra!
Suppose all sentient beings in the world were to fully accomplish the dharma of the eighth stage;

the precepts possessed by them would not equal even one hundredth part, nor one thousandth part, nor even one *upaniṣad* part of a single bodhisattva precept taken at the initial moment of generating the mind of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment by those bodhisattvas."
At that time, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra said to Śāriputra:
"I now wish to ask the Venerable One about the meaning and purpose of the eighth [topic]. Would you perhaps grant me permission to explain this meaning and purpose for me?"
Śāriputra said: “Ask whatever you wish;
once I have heard it, I shall explain it for you.
Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra said:
"Is it that the aggregate of form itself is the eighth? Śāriputra replied, "No!"
"Venerable One!
Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra said,
"Is there an eighth [consciousness] that exists apart from the aggregate of form?"
Śāriputra said: "No, venerable friend!"
Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra asked:
"Is it that the aggregates of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are themselves the eighth? Śāriputra replied:
"No, Venerable One! Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra replied.
"Is there an eighth [aggregate] apart from the aggregates of feeling, perception,
mental formations, and consciousness? Śāriputra replied, "No!"
"Venerable One!
Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra said:
"Is it that the eye-base itself is the eighth?"
Śāriputra said: "No, Venerable One!"
Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra said:
“Is there an eighth [element] apart from the sense-base of the eye? Śāriputra replied:
"No, Venerable One! Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra replied.
“Is it that the sense bases of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind are themselves the eighth? Śāriputra replied, “No!”
"Venerable One!
Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra said:
"Is there an eighth [base] that exists apart from the bases of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind?"
Śāriputra said: "No, Venerable One!"
Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra said:
"Is it that the sphere of form itself is the eighth? Śāriputra said:
"No, Venerable One! Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra replied.
"Is there an eighth [consciousness] apart from the sphere of form? Śāriputra replied, "No!"
"Venerable One!
Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra said:
"Is it that the spheres of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, and mental phenomena are themselves the eighth?"
Śāriputra said: "No, Venerable One!"
Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra asked:
"Is there an eighth [basis] that exists apart from the bases of sound, odor, taste, touch, and mental phenomena? Śāriputra replied:
"No, Venerable One! Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra replied.
“Is it that the eye-element itself is the eighth? Śāriputra replied, “No!”
"Venerable One!
Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra said:
"Is there an eighth [consciousness] apart from the eye-consciousness?"
Śāriputra said: "No, venerable friend!"
Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra asked,
"Is it that the spheres of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind are themselves the eighth? Śāriputra replied:
"No, Venerable One! Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra replied.
“Is there an eighth element apart from the elements of the ear, nose, tongue,
body, and mind? Śāriputra replied, “No!”
"Venerable One!
Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra said,
"Is it that the form realm itself is the eighth?"
Śāriputra said, “No, venerable friend!”
Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra asked:
"Is there an eighth [existence] apart from the realm of form? Śāriputra replied:
"No, Venerable One! Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra replied.
“Is it that the realms of sound, odor, taste, touch, and mental phenomena are themselves the eighth? Śāriputra replied, “No!”
"Venerable One!
Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra said,
"Is there an eighth [element] apart from the realms of sound, odor, taste, touch, and mental phenomena?"
Śāriputra said: “No, venerable friend!”
Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra asked,
"Is it that the eye-consciousness element itself is the eighth? Śāriputra replied:
"No, Venerable One! Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra replied.
“Is there an eighth [element] apart from the eye-consciousness element? Śāriputra replied, “No!”
"Venerable One!
Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra said:
"Is it that the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind-consciousness elements themselves constitute the eighth?"
Śāriputra said: “No, venerable friend!”
Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra asked:
"Is there an eighth [consciousness] that exists apart from the spheres of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mental consciousness? Śāriputra replied:
"No, Venerable One! Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra replied.
"Is it that eye-contact itself is the eighth? Śāriputra replied, "No!"
"Venerable One!
Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra said,
"Is there an eighth [element] apart from eye-contact?"
Śāriputra said: "No, Venerable One!"
Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra asked,
"Is it that the contact of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind is itself the eighth? Śāriputra replied:
"No, Venerable One! Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra replied.
“Is there an eighth [contact] apart from the contacts of the ear, nose, tongue,
body, and mind? Śāriputra replied, “No!”
"Venerable One!
Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra said:
"Is it that the various feelings produced with eye-contact as a condition constitute the eighth [consciousness]?"
Śāriputra said: “No, venerable friend!”
Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra said:
"Is there an eighth [consciousness] apart from the feelings produced with eye-contact as a condition? Śāriputra replied:
"No, Venerable One! Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra replied.
“Is it that the various feelings produced with ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind-contact as conditions constitute the eighth? Śāriputra replied, “No!”
"Venerable One!
Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra said,
"Is there an eighth [feeling] apart from those feelings produced with ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind-contact as conditions?"
Śāriputra said: "No, venerable friend!"
Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra asked:
"Is it that the earth element itself is the eighth? Śāriputra replied:
"No, Venerable One! Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra replied.
"Is there an eighth [element] apart from the earth element? Śāriputra replied, "No!"
"Venerable One!
Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra said:
"Is it that the elements of water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness themselves constitute the eighth?"
Śāriputra said: “No, venerable friend!”
Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra asked:
"Is there an eighth element that exists apart from the elements of water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness? Śāriputra replied:
"No, Venerable One! Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra replied.
"If that is so, Venerable Sir, what dharma do you designate as the eighth?
How may I understand the meaning and intent of what the Venerable has said, so that I may receive and uphold it correctly?"

Śāriputra said: "If, within the equality of all phenomena, one knows that equality with wisdom as it truly is and realizes that equality, then by means of this wisdom, what was to be done is finished."

Within this, I do not perceive an eighth [consciousness], nor do I perceive the wisdom that knows equality; since herein there is no self and nothing belonging to a self, how can one raise objections or interrogate regarding it?
Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra said:
"How is it that what the Venerable One has previously stated does not contradict what you have stated later?
Namely, you previously said:"

"Compared to a single bodhisattva precept at the moment of first generating the mind for unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment among all the bodhisattvas who have generated that mind, all the pure ethical discipline possessed by those in the eighth stage does not equal even one hundredth part, nor one thousandth part, nor even an *upaniṣad* part."
"Now you further say:
'In this regard, I do not perceive at all an eighth [consciousness] nor its cognition. Śāriputra said:
"What I have previously taught was for beginners, not for those who have already entered into the state of equality;
what I have previously taught was intended to lead sentient beings to enter the True Dharma, not for those who have already entered into the state of equality;

what I have previously taught was intended to cause sentient beings to know that the practice of the Mahāyāna transcends the two vehicles, and did not speak of the true nature of the equality of all phenomena."

What I have previously stated was intended to cause sentient beings to realize, as it truly is, the excellence of the pure precepts of the Buddha-vehicle and the Great Vehicle; therefore, I made this declaration:

even if all sentient beings in the world were to fully accomplish the state of an eighth-rank practitioner, the precepts possessed by them would not equal even one-hundredth part, nor one-thousandth part, nor even one *upaniṣad* (infinitesimal) part of the single bodhisattva precept of a bodhisattva who has first resolved to attain unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.
What contradiction is there in not saying that the true nature of all phenomena is equal and devoid of self and what belongs to a self?

Furthermore, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra, the pure ethical discipline of all stream-enterers, once-returners, non-returners, arhats, and pratyekabuddhas does not equal even one hundredth part, nor one thousandth part, nor even an *upaniṣad* part of the single bodhisattva precept of those bodhisattvas who have first resolved to attain unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment.
"Venerable ones, you should know this:

those who wish to claim that the pure ethical discipline of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas is superior to the ethical discipline of bodhisattvas, are effectively wishing to claim that the pure ethical discipline of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas is superior to the ethical discipline of the Tathāgata. You should know that such individuals seek to dispute with the Tathāgata regarding their relative superiority or inferiority."
For example, if someone were to quarrel with a prince, one should know that person intends to quarrel with the king;

likewise, if anyone should wish for the pure ethical discipline of śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas to surpass the ethical discipline of a bodhisattva, they would thereby wish for all the pure ethical discipline of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas to surpass the ethical discipline of the Tathāgata. One should know that such persons intend to dispute with the Tathāgata regarding their relative superiority or inferiority.
For what reason? Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra!
Because the dharmas of all bodhisattvas are invincible, and because bodhisattvas are true sons of the Dharma King.
"Furthermore, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra!
It is as if there were a person who was neither handless nor footless, yet made this claim:
'I am able to cross over to the other shore of the great ocean.'"
"Those words are empty and lack true meaning; they are spoken out of overweening pride (*adhimāna*).
Likewise, if any śrāvaka or pratyekabuddha should say:
'The precepts I possess are superior to the bodhisattva precepts.'"
"You should know that those words are entirely devoid of true meaning.
Why is this? O Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra!"
Because the merit of a bodhisattva is like the great ocean.
It is like that foolish person who, having no hands or feet at all, says:
"I can cross over the great ocean."
"In this way, those who are inclined toward the two vehicles truly lack the sublime merits of a bodhisattva, yet they say:
'I am superior to the pure precepts of a bodhisattva.'"
"That is impossible. Why is this so, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra?"
“Because the pure ethical discipline of a bodhisattva is without limit.
Then, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra asked the venerable Śāriputra:
“For what reason do you say that the pure ethical discipline of a bodhisattva is without limit?”

Śāriputra said: “Because the pure ethical discipline of a bodhisattva can universally liberate immeasurable sentient beings from the evil of violating precepts, and can universally establish immeasurable sentient beings in pure ethical discipline.”
Then, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra again asked the venerable Śāriputra:
"Venerable sir, what is the metaphorical designation for 'one who violates the precepts' as spoken by you? Śāriputra replied:

“Grasping at ‘I’ and ‘mine,’ as well as other afflictions, are called the evil of violating morality. That is to say, the notion of maintenance, the notion of a self, the notion of a sentient being, the notion of a life-principle, the notion of a living being, the notion of a nourisher, the notion of a person, the notion of an individual, the notion of existence, or the notion of non-existence—all such notions and other afflictions are designations for the evil of violating morality.”

The pure ethical discipline (*śīla*) manifested by a bodhisattva is capable of universally liberating immeasurable sentient beings from such transgressions of ethical discipline as have been described; thus, its measure is without limit.

Furthermore, all the pure ethical discipline possessed by bodhisattvas is capable of universally establishing immeasurable sentient beings in pure ethical discipline. Therefore, the pure ethical discipline obtained by a bodhisattva who abides in the Mahāyāna is of limitless measure, beyond the reach of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, and universally surpasses the pure ethical discipline of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
Furthermore, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra!

All bodhisattvas are said to be universally superior to all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, because they cultivate the perfection of ethical discipline and dedicate it toward the pursuit of the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna).
At that time, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra asked Śāriputra:
"In what way can the impure pure precepts of a bodhisattva surpass the pure precepts of the two vehicles, which are free from outflows?"

Śāriputra said: “The untainted pure precepts of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas seek only their own benefit and are dedicated toward nirvāṇa; the pure precepts of a bodhisattva, however, are universally for the sake of liberating immeasurable sentient beings and are dedicated toward unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment. Therefore, all the pure precepts possessed by a bodhisattva surpass the untainted pure precepts of the two vehicles.”
"Furthermore, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra!

If bodhisattvas, with a mind that establishes limits, bring about the benefit of sentient beings and thereby induce pure ethical discipline, the pure ethical discipline thus aroused by those bodhisattvas does not surpass the untainted (anāsrava) pure ethical discipline of the two vehicles; it is not called the perfection of ethical discipline (śīlapāramitā)."

However, because the minds of bodhisattvas are without limitation and they seek great enlightenment in order to universally deliver immeasurable sentient beings, they give rise to pure ethical discipline; therefore, the pure ethical discipline produced by a bodhisattva surpasses the untainted pure ethical discipline of the two vehicles and is called the perfection of pure ethical discipline (*śīlapāramitā*).
"Furthermore, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra!
Just as when the sun’s orb rises and emits great radiance, the lights of fireflies and the like are all eclipsed;

so too, when a bodhisattva practices the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīlapāramitā*) and dedicates it toward the pursuit of the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*), it universally surpasses all the ethical discipline of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas who dedicate it toward nirvāṇa."
"Furthermore, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra!
Just as when the lunar orb emerges and radiates great light, all the starlight is eclipsed and outshone;

so too, when a bodhisattva practices the perfection of ethical discipline and dedicates it toward the pursuit of the knowledge of all modes, it universally surpasses all the ethical discipline of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas dedicated toward nirvāṇa."
"Furthermore, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra!

When a bodhisattva, recollecting the Tathāgata, dedicates [their merit] toward seeking the knowledge of all-knowledge (sarvajñajñāna), and by generating a mind of superior corresponding power, attains the perfection of ethical discipline (śīlapāramitā), at that time they are said to be practicing their own proper sphere, universally surpassing all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas."
Then, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra asked the venerable Śāriputra:
"At what time is a bodhisattva not manifesting the arousal of the mind of omniscience—at that time, by what name is the bodhisattva designated?"

Śāriputra said: "If at any time a bodhisattva does not manifest the arousal of the mind of omniscience (*sarvajñatā-citta*), then at that time the bodhisattva is said to abide in a continuity of neutral (*avyākṛta*) mind. At such a time, it should be known that the bodhisattva is still called one who possesses the precepts; he has not yet violated the bodhisattva precepts, nor is he said to have abandoned the pure bodhisattva morality."

If at any time a bodhisattva does not manifest the arousal of the mind of omniscience, then that bodhisattva turns toward the level of a śrāvaka or a pratyekabuddha; at that time, the bodhisattva abandons the bodhisattva level and loses their own sphere of practice.

If bodhisattvas, for as long as they direct their merit toward the level of a śrāvaka or a pratyekabuddha, then for that same duration those bodhisattvas should be known as having died in regard to the Unsurpassed Vehicle; although it is not an actual death, it receives the name of "death."
It is like a master illusionist or his disciple who, taking a child by the hand, leads him up a high ladder and then makes it appear that the child’s body parts fall off one by one;
at that time, the child’s kinsmen all think he has died, and they lament, wail, and give rise to great anguish, crying out:
"How is it that this child has suddenly perished? We, his relatives, shall have no way to see him again!"

The Bodhisattva is likewise: one should know that to abandon great enlightenment and retreat to abide in the stage of a Śrāvaka or a Pratyekabuddha is like losing all-knowledge (sarvajñatā), which is equivalent to death; just as those relatives, although the child has not lost his life, nevertheless conceive the notion that he is dead.
"Furthermore, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra! What do you think?
What is the distinction between the pure ethical discipline of a bodhisattva and the pure ethical discipline possessed by ordinary beings, śrāvakas, and pratyekabuddhas?"
Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra said:
“In this way, the true suchness and the dharma-nature of all these precepts are truly without distinction. Śāriputra said:

"Although the suchness and the dharmatā of these various precepts are without distinction, it can nevertheless be said that they possess distinct characteristics. How should these distinct characteristics be explained?"
Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra said:
"Just as bodhisattvas seek to realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening, whereas ordinary beings, śrāvakas, and pratyekabuddhas do not;
so too, the pure ethical discipline possessed by bodhisattvas is said to differ from those other forms of discipline."

Śāriputra said: "Because of the pure ethical discipline possessed by this bodhisattva, it surpasses the pure ethical discipline of all ordinary beings, śrāvakas, and pratyekabuddhas. That is to say, the bodhisattva’s ethical discipline—which is dedicated toward the pursuit of the knowledge of all modes—is called the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīlapāramitā*); other forms of discipline are not so. This is what constitutes the distinction."
Why is this? Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra!

The pure ethical discipline of a bodhisattva universally surpasses that of all sentient beings throughout the trichiliocosm and other immeasurable, boundless realms; with the exception of the pure ethical discipline possessed by the Buddha, the World-Honored One, it is the most excellent and foremost among all other forms of pure ethical discipline.
Why is this so? Because the pure ethical discipline of a bodhisattva can lead immeasurable and boundless sentient beings to liberation from saṃsāra and all evil destinies.

For this reason, among the pure ethical disciplines of all ordinary beings, śrāvakas, and pratyekabuddhas, the pure ethical discipline of a bodhisattva is the most supreme, the most excellent, the most honored, the most exalted, the most sublime, the most exquisite, the highest, and the unsurpassed.
"Furthermore, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra!
Just as the King of Snowy Mountains possesses the qualities of a mountain king while other mountains do not;
if one possesses these qualities, he receives the name 'Mountain King,' but if one does not possess these qualities, the title of 'King' is not established."

In this way, all the pure ethical discipline (*śīla*) of a bodhisattva is dedicated toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment; because it does not depart from the pursuit of the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*), it is called the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīlapāramitā*).

The pure ethical discipline of pratyekabuddhas, śrāvakas, and ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), however, does not seek to dedicate itself toward unsurpassed enlightenment and remains far removed from the sought-after knowledge of all modes; therefore, it is not called the perfection of ethical discipline.
"Furthermore, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra!
All the pure precepts possessed by the assembly of bodhisattvas universally surpass all the pure precepts possessed by ordinary beings, śrāvakas, and pratyekabuddhas."
Then, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra addressed the venerable Śāriputra, saying:
"For what reason does the pure ethical discipline of the bodhisattva mahāsattvas universally surpass the pure ethical discipline of ordinary beings, śrāvakas, and pratyekabuddhas?"

Śāriputra said: “The pure ethical discipline of a bodhisattva is universally for the benefit and happiness of all sentient beings, and is dedicated toward the pursuit of the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna). Ordinary beings, śrāvakas, and pratyekabuddhas do not act in this way; therefore, all the pure ethical discipline possessed by a bodhisattva universally surpasses all the pure ethical discipline possessed by ordinary beings, śrāvakas, and pratyekabuddhas.”
Then, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra praised the venerable Śāriputra, saying:
“Excellent! Excellent!”
So it is! So it is! It is exactly as you have said.
Thus he praised the pure ethical discipline of bodhisattvas, causing the assembly of bodhisattvas to become even more diligent in upholding all the pure ethical discipline possessed by bodhisattvas.

Venerable sir, you must surely be speaking through the Buddha’s spiritual power regarding the pure ethical discipline of all bodhisattvas, which universally surpasses the pure ethical discipline of ordinary beings, śrāvakas, and pratyekabuddhas.
At that time, the Buddha addressed Ānanda, saying:

"You should receive and uphold all the teachings on the dharmas associated with the perfection of ethical discipline belonging to the assembly of bodhisattvas, just as they have been expounded by Śāriputra and Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra; such an exposition is certainly not false."
Suppose someone were to take Mount Sumeru, the King of Mountains, and ascend to the Brahma world to hurl it downward;
as soon as he had hurled it, he uttered this word of truth:
"If the bodhisattva precepts are universally superior to the pure precepts of ordinary beings, śrāvakas, and pratyekabuddhas, may this king of mountains remain suspended in mid-air."
Having spoken thus, he remained stationary and did not fall.
Why is this? Ānanda!

Among all the bodhisattva precepts, with the exception of the Tathāgata’s precepts, these other pure precepts—whether contaminated or uncontaminated—are the most supreme, the most excellent, the most honored, the most exalted, the most wondrous, the most subtle, the highest, and the unsurpassed.

At that time, Śāriputra, by the supernatural power of the Buddha, he saw a buddha-field in the eastern direction, a hundred thousand world-systems away from this buddha-field, wherein a Tathāgata was currently expounding the sublime Dharma for a vast assembly of humans, devas, and others.
At that time, the Buddha addressed Śāriputra, saying:
"Do you see, to the east, beyond hundreds of thousands of worlds, a buddha-field where a Tathāgata currently resides, preaching the True Dharma to an immeasurable assembly?"
Śāriputra said: “Indeed! I have seen it!”
"I do not yet know that realm or what that Buddha is named.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Śāriputra:
"That Buddha-world is named Bright Lamp (Pradīpa). The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha who currently teaches the Dharma therein is titled Moonlight (Candraprabha)."

That Buddha had a śrāvaka disciple named Yugandhara, foremost in supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*). By means of his supernormal power, he went to another world-system, plucked up Mount Sumeru, the king of mountains, with his right hand, ascended to the Brahma-world, and cast it down.
As soon as he had thrown it down, he uttered this word of solemn truth (*satyavacana*):

"If the bodhisattva precepts—excluding the Tathāgata’s precepts—are the most supreme, the most excellent, the most honored, the highest, the most wonderful, the most subtle, the most superior, and the unsurpassed among all other pure precepts, whether with outflows (*sāsrava*) or without outflows (*anāsrava*), and if what I have said is not false, may this king of mountains remain suspended in mid-air."
Having spoken thus, he remained there and did not descend further.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Śāriputra:
“Do you see that King of Mountains, Sumeru, abiding in mid-air and no longer descending?”
Then, Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“I have seen them,
World-Honored One!”
Again, he addressed Śāriputra, saying:

"As for that king of mountains now abiding in space, it is because it relies upon the pure precepts possessed by a bodhisattva—precepts which, with the exception of the Tathāgata’s own, are more truthful than those of ordinary beings, śrāvakas, and others, and thus universally surpass them; therefore, I say that my words are certainly not false."

Among the assembly of that Buddha, the śrāvaka disciples, by means of their supernormal powers, travel to other worlds, pluck up Mount Sumeru with their right hands, ascend to the Brahma-world and cast it down; having cast it down, they utter words of solemn truth: "If what I say is certainly not false, may this king of mountains remain suspended in space as witness."
At that time, a śrāvaka disciple of that Tathāgata, relying upon the bodhisattva precepts, made a solemn declaration of truth, causing that king of mountains to return to its original place.
When Śāriputra saw this, he praised him, saying:
"How extraordinary!"
“World-Honored One!
What you have said is true and authentic.
The power of the bodhisattva precepts is inconceivable; none in all the worlds can equal it.”
Then, Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“If there were anyone who wished to surpass the bodhisattva precepts, one should know that they wish to surpass the precepts of the Tathāgata.”
Why is this so? Apart from the precepts of the Tathāgata, there is truly nothing that can surpass the Bodhisattva precepts.
If one cultivates the pure precepts of a bodhisattva to perfection, one is then named a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha; therefore, the Bodhisattva precepts are unsurpassable.
Then, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra asked the venerable Śāriputra:
"Is it not difficult for a Bodhisattva to fall away from his pure ethical discipline? Śāriputra replied:
"It is certain that there is no bodhisattva who dwells with the bodhisattva-mind and yet undergoes regression; if there were such regression, one would not be a bodhisattva.
Just as a skilled archer whose arrows do not hit the mark should be known as no true archer, so it is with the bodhisattva:

if one cannot give rise to the mind associated with the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*), and though one diligently practices the perfections of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom, does not dedicate these toward the knowledge of all modes, one should know that such a person is not a bodhisattva endowed with the precepts."
Furthermore, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra!
Suppose there is a bodhisattva who cultivates various merits, yet does not understand how a bodhisattva dedicates them toward omniscience (sarvajñajñāna).
Instead, they take the merits belonging to the levels of śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas as being the very omniscience they seek.
You should know that such individuals may still be called bodhisattvas endowed with ethical discipline. Why is this?
O Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra!

That bodhisattva lacks skillful means and does not understand how to dedicate [merit] toward omniscience; yet, because their intention remains unbroken—taking as the object of their pursuit all the merits belonging to the stages of the two vehicles while regarding them as the sought-after omniscience—they are also called a bodhisattva endowed with ethical discipline.

Because the upholding of the bodhisattva precepts is due to the dedication toward the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna), it is called "upholding the bodhisattva precepts," thereby encompassing the perfection of ethical discipline (śīlapāramitā).

If, at a later time, they encounter a virtuous friend who can direct their focus toward the true knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna) and dedicate it toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, they will certainly realize that knowledge of all modes.

There are two types of bodhisattvas who both realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment:
first, there is the bodhisattva who, by virtue of possessing skillful means, swiftly realizes unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
2. Furthermore, there are bodhisattvas who, due to a lack of skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*), are slow to realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*).
Venerable one, you should know this:
it would be better for a bodhisattva to be slow in realizing unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment than to fall into the level of a śrāvaka or a pratyekabuddha.
If bodhisattvas seek unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment swiftly, it should be understood that two possibilities exist herein:
first, if they lack skillful means, they will realize the limit of reality and fall into the stage of the two vehicles.
Second, if one possesses skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*), one will swiftly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*).

It is like a heap of various treasures within a house on fire; suppose there is a person seeking treasure who enters this burning house. At that time, that person may be subject to two possible outcomes:
first, if they lack skillful means, they will perish in the burning house.
Second, if one possesses skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*), one emerges carrying the jewels.
In this same way, it should be understood that for a bodhisattva who swiftly seeks unexcelled, perfect enlightenment, two possibilities exist herein:
first, if one lacks skillful means, one will realize the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) and fall to the level of the two vehicles, like being within a burning house.
Second, if one possesses skillful means, one will swiftly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, like extracting a treasure from its container.

Therefore, you should know that it is better to be a bodhisattva who realizes unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment slowly than to be one who seeks speedily and falls into the stages of the two vehicles.
Then, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra asked the venerable Śāriputra:
"Is the swift realization of the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi) not indeed the skillful means (upāyakauśalya) of a bodhisattva? Śāriputra replied:
"To swiftly realize the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) is not the skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*) of a bodhisattva. Why is this?

To fall into the stages of the two vehicles is not the natural outflow (*niṣyanda*) of skillful means; rather, it is the fruit of the natural outflow of a lack of skillful means, for one thereby regresses from the great enlightenment (*mahābodhi*) that was sought."

Now, when a bodhisattva seeks great enlightenment for the benefit of sentient beings, they do not seek the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi). Therefore, the realization of the limit of reality is not the fruit of skillful means.
"Furthermore, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra!..."
If bodhisattvas think to themselves, "I am able to practice giving,
whereas other bodhisattvas cannot," these bodhisattvas act in an improper manner;
because they act improperly, their ethical discipline is impaired, and this is not called the perfection of generosity (dānapāramitā).
"Furthermore, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra!
If various bodhisattvas should think thus:
'I am able to guard the precepts, whereas other bodhisattvas are not.'"

"These bodhisattvas practice in what is not the proper sphere; because they practice in what is not the proper sphere, their precepts are impaired and deficient, and thus it is not called the perfection of pure ethical discipline (śīlapāramitā).
Furthermore, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra!"
If bodhisattvas think, "I am able to practice patience, whereas other bodhisattvas cannot," these bodhisattvas act in an improper manner;
because they act improperly, their ethical discipline is impaired, and this is not called the perfection of patience (kṣānti-pāramitā).
"Furthermore, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra!
If various bodhisattvas should think thus:

"Furthermore, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra!
If various bodhisattvas should think thus:
'I am able to cultivate wisdom, whereas other bodhisattvas cannot.'"

"These bodhisattvas practice in what is not the proper place; because they practice in what is not the proper place, their precepts are impaired and deficient, and thus it is not called the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
Furthermore, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra!"

whereas other bodhisattvas cannot," these bodhisattvas are practicing in an improper sphere.

"Venerable one, you should know this:
