For what reason? Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra!
A bodhisattva should not desire to surpass another bodhisattva; a bodhisattva should not treat another bodhisattva with contempt; a bodhisattva should not seek to subjugate another bodhisattva.
"A Bodhisattva should honor and revere other Bodhisattvas just as one would honor and revere a Tathāgata.
At that time, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra asked Śāriputra:
"Should a Bodhisattva only honor Bodhisattvas, or should they also honor all other sentient beings?"
Śāriputra said: "The assembly of bodhisattvas should universally revere all sentient beings; that is to say, just as bodhisattvas revere the Tathāgata, so too should they revere other bodhisattvas;
and just as they revere bodhisattvas, so too should they revere other sentient beings, with no distinction in their minds."
For what reason? Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra!
Toward all sentient beings, the assembly of bodhisattvas should maintain a humble mind, should be deeply respectful, should grant them autonomy, and should remain free from arrogance.
In this way, a bodhisattva should regard all sentient beings with a profound heart of reverence, as if they were Buddhas or bodhisattvas. Such a bodhisattva should think:

"When I realize unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment, I shall preach the essential points of the profound Dharma for sentient beings, so that they may sever their afflictions and attain parinirvāṇa, or attain the ultimate peace and happiness of bodhi, or be liberated from the sufferings of the evil realms."
"Furthermore, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra!
A bodhisattva such as this should give rise to a mind of loving-kindness toward sentient beings; with a mind free from pride toward all sentient beings, they should form this thought:
'I shall cultivate and train in skillful means so that all sentient beings may attain the most supreme nature.'"
Why is this so? Because the primary nature is what is called the Buddha-nature; I shall employ skillful means to cause all sentient beings to attain Buddhahood.

Thus, a bodhisattva gives rise to a mind of loving-kindness toward all classes of sentient beings, desiring that they all may occupy the rank of Dharma King. This rank of Dharma King is most excellent and most venerable; therein, both with respect to the Dharma and to sentient beings, one attains mastery. For this reason, the assembly of Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas should universally revere all sentient beings, for their mind of loving-kindness is all-pervasive and without discrimination, as the Tathāgata’s Dharmakāya pervades all things.
Then, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra asked the venerable Śāriputra:
"How does a bodhisattva form this thought:

'I shall honor all sentient beings; once I have realized unexcelled, perfect enlightenment, I shall instruct and teach all sentient beings so that they all realize the most supreme nature and all attain the station of the Dharma King'?"
"Just as a master illusionist or his disciple might, at a crossroads, conjure by magic a great king and a fourfold army, brave and invincible; yet that illusory king does not think:
'I now possess a fourfold army of brave soldiers whose power is difficult to resist.'"
The fourfold illusory army does not think:
"We all belong to the Great King; we move according to his will. Why is this?

Śāriputra! In this regard, all things—whether kings or armies—are not truly existent; they entirely lack intrinsic nature (svabhāva). They are not subsumed within anything that possesses real intrinsic nature.
As the Blessed One has taught that all phenomena are like illusions, so too are all sentient beings. Since all are like illusions, who is there to be honored by whom?
And who, moreover, can cause another to attain the supreme nature?
"Residing on the throne of the Dharma King,
what kind of Dharma does he teach? Śāriputra replied, "It is so!"
Thus it is! Sentient beings and all phenomena are entirely like illusions.

It should be known that herein, the illusory Bodhisattva reveres all illusory sentient beings, instructing and teaching them through skillful means so that they may attain the supreme illusory Buddha-nature and dwell upon the throne of the Dharma King to preach the illusory Dharma.
Nevertheless, although bodhisattvas form such thoughts, they do not grasp at anything therein at all.

If bodhisattvas have even the slightest perception regarding phenomena, those bodhisattvas are not practicing the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*); when, however, bodhisattvas have no perception whatsoever regarding phenomena, at that time the bodhisattvas are not separated from the perfection of wisdom.

Thus, through skillful means, although these bodhisattvas practice the perfection of diligence and transform sentient beings so that they attain buddhahood, they do not perceive any phenomena at all. That is to say, they do not perceive even the slightest portion of a dharma-nature that can truly cause others to attain the supreme nature, nor do they perceive even the slightest portion of a dharma-nature that can truly cause others to occupy the rank of Dharma King; yet, despite this lack of perception, they do not regress.

It should be known that Bodhisattvas are able to don the vast armor of diligence without any attachment whatsoever. This means that although Bodhisattvas know the rank of the Dharma King is entirely like an illusion and lacks any real existence, they are nonetheless able to seek and advance toward it with unremitting diligence; and while they diligently seek the fruit of Buddhahood, they perceive no phenomena at all within all dharmas; and though they perceive nothing, they do not regress.

In this way, although the bodhisattva knows that gods, humans, asuras, and so forth are all subject to decay and destruction, they harbor no notion of decay and destruction therein, for they have realized that all things are like illusions.

Thus, through skillful means, the bodhisattva seeks to realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, desiring to teach the Dharma of tranquility to sentient beings. This means that although all phenomena are proclaimed through various skillful means by means of collections of names, phrases, and syllables, the intrinsic nature of phenomena is ultimately inexpressible.
"Furthermore, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra!
The nature of all phenomena (dharmatā) cannot be demonstrated and cannot be proclaimed.
When a bodhisattva realizes great awakening (mahābodhi), although they teach the nature of all phenomena for the sake of sentient beings, they maintain this thought:"
“I have not attained anything at all regarding enlightenment, nor have I ever proclaimed any dharma for the sake of sentient beings.
Although I have realized unsurpassed enlightenment, this enlightenment is in fact not to be realized;
although I have proclaimed the nature of all dharmas, the nature of all dharmas is in fact inexpressible.”
"Both the speaker and that which is spoken lack intrinsic nature; likewise, neither the realizer nor that which is realized can be apprehended.

Therefore, when bodhisattva-mahāsattvas wish to realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, they should not cling to any phenomena. Although they have no clinging, they do not regress; because they do not regress, their minds do not sink; and because their minds do not sink, they gather and refine diligence. This is the perfection of diligence (vīrya-pāramitā).

Furthermore, by means of the perfection of diligence, one dedicates [the merit] toward the pursuit of the knowledge of all-knowledge, thereby fulfilling the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīla-pāramitā*).

Furthermore, by means of the perfection of ethical discipline, one dedicates [the merit] toward the pursuit of the knowledge of all-knowledge, causing this perfection of ethical discipline to become increasingly superior, increasingly augmented, increasingly luminous, and increasingly pure.

In this way, when a bodhisattva practices and trains in the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīlapāramitā*), it swiftly becomes perfected, increased, superior, luminous, and pure; all of this is due to the bodhisattva’s dedication (*pariṇāmanā*) directed toward the pursuit of the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*).
Then, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra asked the venerable Śāriputra:
"If all phenomena are like illusory things and are not real at all, how can the bodhisattva’s dedication toward the pursuit of the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna) be established?"

Śāriputra said: “If even a slight portion of all phenomena were truly existent and not like illusory things, then bodhisattvas would ultimately be unable to dedicate themselves toward the pursuit of the knowledge of all modes.
Because there is not even the slightest truly existent thing among all phenomena that is not like an illusion, bodhisattvas dedicate themselves toward the pursuit of the knowledge of all modes.”

In this way, when a bodhisattva possesses the capacity to dedicate [merit] toward the pursuit of omniscience with tireless diligence, it should be understood that this capacity arises from their thorough realization that all phenomena are not real, being like illusions and like magical transformations; this is precisely the bodhisattva’s perfection of diligence (vīrya-pāramitā).
Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra said:

"If it is so that a bodhisattva possesses the capability to dedicate [merit] toward the pursuit of the knowledge of all modes with diligent effort and without weariness, what kind of dharma-action constitutes this 'capability' of which you speak?"
"What is this diligence that is capable of being cultivated in such a way?
Śāriputra replied, "Capability is the activity performed through skillful means."
A bodhisattva must rely on skillful means to know that all phenomena are like illusory phenomena.
Abiding in skillful means, the bodhisattva neither fears the emptiness of phenomena nor falls into the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*).

It is, for example, like a person standing on the summit of a high mountain, firmly grasping a light and sturdy parasol with both hands; standing on the edge of a mountain peak with feet raised and neck extended, he looks down at a steep, precipitous, and bottomless abyss below.
Held and guided by the power of the wind supporting the parasol, although he stands on a dangerous cliff, he does not fall.

In the same way, a bodhisattva, sustained by the power of skillful means, great compassion, and prajñā, although he contemplates all phenomena as they truly are—as illusory, false appearances whose intrinsic nature is empty and quiescent—his mind is entirely free from inferiority or fear, yet he does not realize the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi).
Why is this? Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra!
These bodhisattvas, sustained by the power of skillful means, great compassion, and prajñā, do not fear the emptiness of phenomena nor do they realize the limit of reality.
Just as one holding a parasol while looking down upon steep peaks and crags perceives perilous, precipitous pits without fear or falling;

so too, the assembly of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, donning firm armor and embracing skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*), relying upon the accomplishment of the foremost, perfect perfection of ethical discipline (*śīla-pāramitā*), though they seek unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, do not perceive any dharma as having been realized or being realized.

It should be understood that all such perfections of ethical discipline (*śīlapāramitā*) of a bodhisattva, being embraced by skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*), are able to lead to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment (*anuttarasamyaksambodhi*).

In this way, because they are sustained by skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*), bodhisattvas never remain apart from the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*) that are to be studied. By not remaining apart from these six perfections to be studied, these bodhisattvas gradually draw near to the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvajñajñāna*) and surpass all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas. Why is this?
Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra!
These bodhisattvas single-mindedly seek all-knowledge as if it were an invaluable jewel.
Furthermore, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra!
Suppose there are two people who, employing great skillful means, enter a deep mountain cave to seek priceless jewels.
Not long after they have entered, they see on both sides various treasures of lesser value, such as gold and silver; seeing them together, they do not take them and continue forward by degrees.

Furthermore, they see on both sides many precious jewels; one, upon seeing them, becomes greedily attached and returns carrying them; the other, upon seeing them, does not take them but proceeds further until reaching a most excellent place where he obtains priceless jewels, which he carries back at will to bring great benefit to many.

In this way, when a bodhisattva employs great skillful means to seek the realization of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, desiring to bring great benefit to sentient beings, there are briefly two ways of entering the Buddha-dharma.

First, there is the bodhisattva who, due to a lack of skillful means, does not become attached to various worldly wholesome dharmas upon hearing them; yet, upon hearing of the merits of the two vehicles, he immediately develops a craving for them. Because of this craving, he diligently pursues them, thereby distancing himself from the sought-after knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*) and falling away from the mind of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
This is like the first person who, seeing a gem of little value, does not covet it, but seeing one of great value, covets and takes it away, only to lose the priceless jewel.

Second, because a bodhisattva possesses skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*), upon first hearing the various mundane wholesome dharmas, their mind does not become stained by craving; subsequently, upon hearing of all the merits of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*), they likewise do not relish them. Because they do not relish them, they do not dwell upon them; because they do not dwell upon them, they do not cultivate them; and since they do not cultivate them, they skillfully abandon them through detachment.

Why is this? These bodhisattvas understand that the worldly wholesome dharmas possess many faults and afflictions; they cannot ultimately accomplish the benefit of oneself and others, and they obstruct the sought-after knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna).

Although the merit and roots of goodness of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas transcend the world, they benefit only themselves and cannot universally benefit all sentient beings; they likewise obstruct the sought-after knowledge of all modes. Therefore, they do not relish them nor contemplate them, and they take no pleasure in cultivating those roots of goodness.
By this means, they transcend the stages of the two vehicles and diligently seek unexcelled, perfect enlightenment, gradually realizing the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*);

just as that latter person, seeing both a low-priced jewel and a high-priced jewel, feels no attachment to either, but gradually penetrates deeper until reaching the most supreme place, where he obtains a priceless jewel and carries it back at will, bringing great benefit to all sentient beings.

"Thus, through such skillful means, the bodhisattva neither becomes stained by attachment to worldly wholesome dharmas nor relishes the teachings of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*). By this, they gradually proceed toward great enlightenment (*mahābodhi*), practicing hundreds of thousands of difficult and painful asceticisms, making offerings to and honoring immeasurable Tathāgatas, maturing sentient beings, and purifying Buddha-fields. Upon reaching ultimate perfection and attaining omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), they bring benefit, peace, and happiness to immeasurable sentient beings, providing vast assistance like a priceless jewel."

Thus, through their skillful means, although these bodhisattvas hear of the various merits of the two vehicles, they understand that none of them are ultimate; though they are able to realize them, they deeply weary of and relinquish them; and though they deeply weary of and relinquish them, they are able to skillfully explain them, benefiting those types of sentient beings through skillful means so that they may practice well and realize the bliss of nirvana.

In this way, through skillful means, the bodhisattva is able to refrain from appropriating the merits of the two vehicles; they diligently practice all bodhisattva deeds, proceed toward the realization of unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment, and bring about the benefit and happiness of all sentient beings.
At that time, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra asked Śāriputra:
"If bodhisattvas abide in the stage of non-retrogression, in what practices should they not indulge with attachment?"
Śāriputra said: "He should not become attached to the six perfections. Why is that?"
Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra!

If one becomes deeply attached to the perfections of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom, the mind becomes defiled; thus, one cannot truly benefit and bring happiness to sentient beings, nor can one purify the Buddha-fields. Consequently, it will take a long time before such a person can realize the sought-after unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Therefore, that bodhisattva should think: "Although I must practice the six perfections with diligent vigor, uninterrupted as if my head were on fire, I must not become attached to them."
"Furthermore, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra!
Those bodhisattvas should not become attached to various contemplations of emptiness. Why is this?
Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra!

If, while contemplating the meditations on inner emptiness, outer emptiness, inner-and-outer emptiness, the emptiness of emptiness, great emptiness, ultimate emptiness, conditioned emptiness, unconditioned emptiness, absolute emptiness, boundless emptiness, dispersed emptiness, non-altering emptiness, essential emptiness, self-characteristic emptiness, common-characteristic emptiness, the emptiness of all phenomena, the emptiness of the unapprehendable, the emptiness of non-existence, the emptiness of intrinsic nature, and the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature, the mind becomes defiled, one will be unable to bring beings benefit and happiness according to reality, nor will one be able to purify the Buddha-fields. Consequently, it will take a long time before one can realize the sought-after unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment; therefore, that bodhisattva should form this thought:

"Although I should diligently and vigorously cultivate these various contemplations on emptiness, practicing them without interruption as if my head were on fire, I must not become attached to or relish them therein."
"Furthermore, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra!
Those bodhisattvas should not become attached to the contemplation of suchness and so forth. Why is this?
Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra!

If one deeply relishes and clings to the contemplation of the true suchness (*tathatā*) of all phenomena, the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), the dharma-nature (*dharmatā*), their non-falsity, their immutability, their equality, their nature of being free from birth, the fixedness of dharma (*dharmaniyāmatā*), the stability of dharma (*dharmasthititā*), the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), the realm of space (*ākāśadhātu*), and the inconceivable realm (*acintyadhātu*), the mind becomes defiled. One will thus be unable to bring benefit and happiness to sentient beings as they truly are, nor will one be able to adorn and purify the Buddha-fields. Consequently, it will take a long time before one can realize the sought-after unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*). Therefore, that bodhisattva should form this thought:

"Although I must diligently and vigorously cultivate the contemplation of such true suchness and so forth, practicing without interruption as if my head were on fire, I must not relish or cling to them therein."
"Furthermore, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra!
Those bodhisattvas should not become attached to the contemplation of dependent origination. Why is this?

Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra! If one becomes deeply attached to this [process], one contemplates that ignorance conditions volitional formations; volitional formations condition consciousness; consciousness conditions name-and-form; name-and-form conditions the six sense bases; the six sense bases condition contact; contact conditions feeling; feeling conditions craving; craving conditions grasping; grasping conditions becoming; becoming conditions birth; and birth conditions old age and death. One then contemplates that with the cessation of ignorance, volitional formations cease, and so on, up to the cessation of birth, whereby old age and death cease. If the mind becomes defiled by such contemplation, one will be unable to bring about the true benefit and happiness of sentient beings, nor will one be able to purify a Buddha-field. Consequently, it will take a long time before one can realize the sought-after unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. Therefore, that bodhisattva should form this thought:

"Although I should diligently and vigorously cultivate such contemplation of dependent origination, practicing it continuously and without interruption as if my head were on fire, I must not become attached to or relish it therein."
"Furthermore, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra!
Those bodhisattvas should not become attached to the contemplation of the noble truths. Why is this?
Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra!

If one becomes deeply attached to the contemplation of the Four Noble Truths—suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path—the mind becomes defiled; one will be unable to bring about the true benefit and happiness of sentient beings, nor will one be able to purify the Buddha-fields. Consequently, it will take a long time before one can realize the sought-after unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

Therefore, that bodhisattva should form this thought: "Although I should diligently and vigorously cultivate the contemplation of these Noble Truths without interruption, as if my head were on fire, I must not become attached to them."
"Furthermore, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra!
Those bodhisattvas should not become attached to the factors conducive to enlightenment (bodhipakṣa-dharma). Why is this?
Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra!

If one becomes deeply attached to the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path, the mind becomes defiled; one will be unable to bring about the welfare and happiness of sentient beings as they truly are, nor will one be able to purify the Buddha-fields. Consequently, it will take a long time before one can realize the sought-after unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

Therefore, that bodhisattva should form this thought: "Although I should diligently and vigorously cultivate these factors conducive to enlightenment without interruption, as if my head were on fire, I must not become attached to them."
"Furthermore, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra!
Those bodhisattvas should not become attached to the flavor of the three gates of liberation. Why is this?
Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra!

If one becomes deeply attached to the gates of liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness—the mind becomes defiled; one will be unable to bring benefit and happiness to sentient beings as they truly are, nor will one be able to adorn and purify the Buddha-fields. Consequently, it will take a long time before such a person can realize the sought-after unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

Therefore, that bodhisattva should form this thought: "Although I must diligently and vigorously cultivate these three gates of liberation without interruption, as if my head were on fire, I must not become attached to them."
"Furthermore, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra!
Those bodhisattvas should not become attached to the flavor of the gateways of dhāraṇīs or the gateways of samādhis. Why is this?
Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra!

If one becomes deeply attached to the gates of dhāraṇī and the gates of samādhi, the mind becomes defiled; one will be unable to bring beings benefit and happiness according to reality, nor will one be able to purify the buddha-fields. Because of this, it will take a long time before one can realize the sought-after unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

Therefore, that bodhisattva should form this thought: "Although I should diligently and vigorously cultivate these gates of dhāraṇī and samādhi without interruption—like one whose head is on fire—I must not become attached to them."
"Furthermore, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra!
Those bodhisattvas should not become attached to the flavors of the dhyānas, the immeasurables, the meditative attainments, or the liberations. Why is this?
Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra!

If one becomes deeply attached to the dhyānas, the immeasurables, the meditative attainments (*samāpatti*), and the liberations (*vimokṣa*), the mind becomes defiled; one will then be unable to bring beings benefit and happiness in accordance with reality, nor will one be able to purify the Buddha-fields. Consequently, it will take a long time before one can realize the sought-after unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*).

Therefore, that bodhisattva should form this thought: "Although I should diligently and vigorously cultivate these dhyānas, immeasurables, meditative attainments, and liberations without interruption—like one whose head is on fire—I must not become attached to them."
"Furthermore, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra!

Those bodhisattvas should not become attached to the spheres of mastery (abhibhvāyatana), the spheres of totality (kṛtsnāyatana), or the nine successive meditative attainments (navānupūrvavihārasamāpatti). Why is this?
Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra!

If one becomes deeply attached to the spheres of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*), the spheres of totality (*kṛtsnāyatana*), and the nine successive attainments (*navānupūrvavihārasamāpatti*), the mind becomes defiled; one will be unable to bring benefit and happiness to sentient beings as they truly are, nor will one be able to purify a Buddha-field. Consequently, it will take a long time before one can realize the sought-after unsurpassed perfect enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*).

Therefore, that bodhisattva should form this thought: "Although I should diligently and vigorously cultivate these spheres of mastery, spheres of totality, and nine successive attainments—doing so without interruption, as if my head were on fire—I must not become attached to them."
"Furthermore, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra!
Those bodhisattvas should not become attached to the taste of the wisdom cultivated through the various stages (bhūmi). Why is this?
Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra!

If one becomes deeply attached to the wisdom cultivated in the various stages (*bhūmi*), the mind becomes defiled; one will be unable to bring benefit and happiness to sentient beings as they truly are, nor will one be able to purify the Buddha-fields. Consequently, it will take a long time before such a person can realize the sought-after unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*).

Therefore, that bodhisattva should reflect: "Although I must practice with diligence and vigor regarding this wisdom of the various stages—cultivating it without interruption like one whose head is on fire—I must not become attached to it."
"Furthermore, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra!
Those bodhisattvas should not become attached to the five eyes or the six supernormal powers. Why is this?
Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra!

If one becomes deeply attached to the five eyes and the six supernormal powers, the mind becomes defiled; one will be unable to bring beings benefit and happiness according to reality, nor will one be able to purify the Buddha-fields. Consequently, it will take a long time before such a person can realize the sought-after unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

Therefore, that bodhisattva should form this thought: "Although I should diligently and vigorously cultivate these five eyes and six supernormal powers without interruption—like one whose head is on fire—I must not become attached to them."
"Furthermore, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra!
Those bodhisattvas should not become attached to the flavors of the Tathāgata’s ten powers, four fearlessnesses, or four analytical knowledges."
Why is this? Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra!

If one becomes deeply attached to the Tathāgata’s ten powers, four fearlessnesses, and four analytical knowledges, the mind becomes defiled; one will then be unable to bring benefit and happiness to sentient beings as they truly are, nor will one be able to purify the Buddha-fields. Consequently, it will take a long time before such a person can realize the sought-after unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. Therefore, that bodhisattva should form this thought:

"Although I should diligently and vigorously cultivate these ten powers of a Tathāgata, the four fearlessnesses, and the four analytical knowledges—practicing them without interruption as if my head were on fire—I must not become attached to or relish them."
"Furthermore, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra!
Those bodhisattvas should not become attached to great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, or great equanimity. Why is this?
Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra!

If one becomes deeply attached to great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, and great equanimity, the mind becomes defiled; thus one cannot truly bring benefit and happiness to sentient beings, nor can one purify the Buddha-fields. Consequently, it will take a long time before one can realize the sought-after unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. Therefore, that bodhisattva should form this thought:

"Although I must diligently and vigorously cultivate such great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, and great equanimity, without interruption as if my head were on fire, I must not become attached to them."
"Furthermore, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra!
Those bodhisattvas should not become attached to the eighteen unique qualities of a buddha. Why is this?
Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra!

If one becomes deeply attached to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha (āveṇika-buddhadharma), the mind becomes defiled; one will be unable to bring benefit and happiness to sentient beings as they truly are, nor will one be able to adorn and purify the buddha-fields. Consequently, it will take a long time before one can realize the sought-after unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment (anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi).

Therefore, that bodhisattva should form this thought: "Although I should diligently and vigorously cultivate these eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha without interruption—like one whose hair is on fire—I must not become attached to them."
"Furthermore, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra!
Those bodhisattvas should not become attached to the quality of non-forgetfulness or the state of constant equanimity. Why is this?
Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra!

If one becomes deeply attached to the quality of non-forgetfulness (*asaṃpramoṣadharma*) and the state of constant equanimity (*upekṣāvihāritā*), the mind becomes defiled; one will be unable to bring benefit and happiness to sentient beings as they truly are, nor will one be able to purify the Buddha-fields. Consequently, it will take a long time before one can realize the sought-after unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*).

Therefore, that bodhisattva should form this thought: "Although I must practice these qualities of non-forgetfulness and constant equanimity with diligent vigor, uninterrupted like one whose hair is on fire, I should not become attached to them."
"Furthermore, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra!
Those bodhisattvas should not become attached to all-knowledge (sarvajñatā), the knowledge of the aspects of the path (mārgākārajñatā), or the knowledge of all aspects (sarvākārajñatā). Why is this?
Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra!

If one becomes deeply attached to all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), the knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*), and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*), the mind becomes defiled; one will be unable to bring about the welfare and happiness of sentient beings as they truly are, nor will one be able to purify the Buddha-fields. Consequently, it will take a long time before one can realize the sought-after unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*).

Therefore, that bodhisattva should form this thought: "Although I should diligently and vigorously cultivate all these—namely, all-knowledge, the knowledge of the aspects of the path, and the knowledge of all aspects—without interruption, like one whose head is on fire, I must not become attached to them."
"Furthermore, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra!
If bodhisattvas wish to realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, they should not engage in such conceptualization as this:
'By means of these pure precepts of a bodhisattva, I shall acquire the primary marks and the secondary signs.'"
If bodhisattvas manifest such discriminative thoughts, it should be known that they have violated the bodhisattva precepts.
Therefore, a bodhisattva should not greedily seek the primary marks and secondary signs, nor should they seek to proceed toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment [based upon them].
If bodhisattvas grasp at the marks and signs while observing the pure precepts, it should be known that they are grasping at the pure precepts and thus commit transgressions;
if bodhisattvas grasp at the pure precepts and commit transgressions, they will certainly be unable to realize the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment they seek.

The Great Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra, Scroll 587. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree. Part Five of the Twelfth Section on the Pāramitā of Pure Ethics. At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Śāriputra:

"You are able to abide thus in sublime wisdom, meaning that you know, according to reality, that such a bodhisattva who clings to pure ethics commits transgressions, whereas such a bodhisattva who does not cling to ethics commits no transgressions."
Then Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“I have faith in the sublime Dharma spoken by the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, and thus I have given rise to this wisdom; it is not that I am able to speak thus on my own authority.”

As I understand the meaning of what the Buddha has taught, if any among the assembly of bodhisattvas should even momentarily give rise to a mind that delights in or praises the stage of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas, it should be known that they have violated the pure bodhisattva precepts;

if any among the assembly of bodhisattvas should even momentarily give rise to a mind that feels weary of or disparages the stage of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas, it should be known that they have violated the pure bodhisattva precepts.

Why is this? If bodhisattvas delight in or praise the stages of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas, they will develop attachment to those stages, fail to seek after the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*), and thereby commit transgressions against the bodhisattva precepts.

If bodhisattvas feel aversion toward or disparage the stages of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas, they will develop contempt for those stages, which obstructs the sought-after knowledge of all modes and constitutes a transgression of the bodhisattva precepts. Therefore, regarding the stages of the two vehicles, bodhisattvas should neither delight in nor praise them, nor should they feel aversion or disparage them.
If bodhisattvas do not respect the stages of the two vehicles, or if they develop attachment to them, you should know that in all such cases they are practicing in an improper sphere (*agocara*).

If bodhisattvas practice in an improper sphere, they should be known as bodhisattvas who have violated their precepts, and they are also called those who grasp at the signs of pure morality; they will be unable to realize the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*). Therefore, regarding the stages of the two vehicles, a bodhisattva should only maintain distance from them, neither praising nor disparaging them.
"If bodhisattvas do not distance themselves from the stages of the two vehicles, they will certainly be unable to attain the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment they seek.
Furthermore, World-Honored One!"

If bodhisattvas give rise to a mind of attachment toward the objects of the five desires, although this is termed improper mental attention (*ayoniśomanasikāra*), it does not significantly obstruct unsurpassed enlightenment (*anuttarasamyaksambodhi*).

Why is this so? Because improper mental attention (*ayoniśo-manasikāra*) falls within the category of afflictions (*kleśa*). It is by means of those afflictions that bodhisattvas undergo various births; whenever and wherever the assembly of bodhisattvas receives such and such bodies in such and such realms of existence, at those times they gradually train in and bring to fulfillment the perfections of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom, as well as the other immeasurable and boundless qualities of a Buddha.

Whenever and wherever they gradually train in and bring to fulfillment the perfections of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom, as well as the other immeasurable and boundless qualities of a Buddha, at those times those bodhisattvas gradually draw near to the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*).
Therefore, World-Honored One, I say that afflictions possess great merit for bodhisattvas, in that they are able to accord with the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna).

If bodhisattvas can perceive that afflictions assist in bringing forth the knowledge of all modes and thus possess great merit for the assembly of bodhisattvas, those bodhisattvas should be known as having already realized skillful means regarding all matters; such bodhisattvas should be known as dwelling securely in the bodhisattva perfection of ethical discipline (śīlapāramitā).
"It should be known that these bodhisattvas do not transgress the bodhisattva precepts, nor do they grasp at or become attached to the pure precepts of a bodhisattva.
At that time, the Buddha praised Śāriputra, saying: "Excellent!"
Excellent! So it is! So it is!

You have skillfully explained that among the assembly of bodhisattvas, there are those who have attachment to pure ethical discipline and those who violate it; and there are those who have no attachment to pure ethical discipline and no violation of it.
"You have demonstrated that the Tathāgata is one who speaks the truth, one who speaks according to the Dharma, and one who is skilled in explaining the Dharma in accordance with the Dharma.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!"
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells securely in the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīla-pāramitā*), they should reflect:

"By the superior power of the perfection of ethical discipline in which I dwell, may the immeasurable sentient beings in the infinite and boundless worlds of the ten directions who lack ethical discipline all obtain it, and may those with corrupt discipline all become free from it;
by the superior power of the perfection of ethical discipline that I study, may I sustain these classes of sentient beings so that they all obtain supreme benefit and happiness."

It should be known that this bodhisattva mahāsattva has accomplished skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*). Whenever he dedicates his own perfection of ethical discipline (*śīlapāramitā*) for the sake of immeasurable sentient beings in immeasurable and boundless worlds, at those times his abiding perfection of ethical discipline increases progressively.
Whenever his abiding perfection of ethical discipline increases progressively, at those times he is further able to gather immeasurable perfections of ethical discipline.

Whenever he is further able to gather immeasurable perfections of ethical discipline, at those times he is further able to gather immeasurable and incalculable sublime qualities of the Buddha-dharma (*buddhadharma*); by this, he swiftly attains the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*).
"Furthermore, Śāriputra!
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva abides in the perfection of ethical discipline (śīla-pāramitā), they should reflect thus:

'By the superior power of the perfection of ethical discipline in which I abide, may all immeasurable sentient beings in the infinite and boundless worlds of the ten directions who have not yet resolved upon unsurpassed bodhicitta, be able to generate that resolve;'"
Those who have already resolved upon unsurpassed bodhicitta shall never again fall back;
and those who have not fallen back from the mind of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment will swiftly be able to fulfill the knowledge of all modes of cognition.

"By means of such skillful means, this bodhisattva mahāsattva dedicates the perfection of ethical discipline to all bodhisattvas. Whenever he dedicates the perfection of ethical discipline, at those times he is never separated from the mind of omniscience;
and whenever he is not separated from the mind of omniscience, at those times he gradually draws near to the wisdom of all-knowledge."

By the superior power of these roots of goodness, this bodhisattva mahāsattva is further able to embrace immeasurable perfections of ethical discipline (*śīlapāramitā*), causing them to gradually increase and expand, and is also able to embrace immeasurable and innumerable subtle and wondrous Buddha-dharmas, causing them to gradually reach fulfillment.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra!

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva, dwelling securely in the perfection of ethical discipline (śīla-pāramitā), were to bestow upon a single bodhisattva the mass of merit derived from his own abiding in the bodhisattva’s perfection of ethical discipline, that would surpass the merit of giving to all sentient beings in worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges who have violated their discipline, causing them all to fully and perfectly uphold pure ethical discipline."

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells securely in the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīlapāramitā*), and dedicates their own abiding in the bodhisattva’s perfection of ethical discipline to all sentient beings of the ten directions, causing them to abide in ethical discipline and remain free from transgressions, the mass of merit (*puṇyaskandha*) thus obtained is immeasurable and boundless.

There is a bodhisattva mahāsattva who dwells securely in the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīlapāramitā*). The mass of merit obtained by giving this very perfection of ethical discipline in which he dwells to a single bodhisattva surpasses the mass of merit obtained by the former bodhisattva a hundredfold, a thousandfold, and even up to an *upaniṣad*-fold.
Why is this? Śāriputra,

it is because this bodhisattva mahāsattva, by means of the perfection of pure ethical discipline in which he himself abides, bestows it upon a single bodhisattva, causing that bodhisattva to embrace all-knowledge (sarvajñajñāna) and also enabling them to maintain all-knowledge.

When this bodhisattva is able both to embrace all-knowledge (sarvajñajñāna) and to sustain all-knowledge, they are then able to embrace and sustain immeasurable and boundless worlds and their immeasurable sentient beings, causing them all to abide in pure ethical discipline and remain free from all transgressions; thus, through such successive stages, they bring about vast benefit.
“Suppose, for example, there is a large house with ten bays supported by a single pillar, where immeasurable sentient beings dwell together, playing, frolicking, and enjoying themselves in delight.
At that time, a violent and wicked man wishes to cut down the pillar. Then, a virtuous person says to the wicked man:

‘Now, within this house there are many kinds of beings who play, frolick, and enjoy themselves in delight. If you cut down this pillar, the house will collapse and crumble, harming the immeasurable lives within it.’”
"In this way, that virtuous person, desiring to bring benefit and happiness to the immeasurable sentient beings dwelling therein, prevents those wicked people from cutting down the pillar.
At that time, a man praised the virtuous person, saying: 'Excellent!'"
"Excellent!
You have now bestowed life, security, and happiness upon immeasurable classes of living beings.

Thus, a bodhisattva who wishes to realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment should, by means of the perfections of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom of the Mahāyāna, as well as other immeasurable and boundless teachings of the Buddha-dharma, provide instruction and guidance so that others may realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, thereby performing great benefit for all sentient beings.

If one were to instruct and admonish by means of the merits and roots of goodness of the Pratyekabuddha and Śrāvaka vehicles, one would thereby obstruct the immeasurable and boundless sublime merits of sentient beings, Arhats, and others.

“If there is a bodhisattva who wishes to realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, and who, by means of the perfections of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom, as well as other immeasurable and boundless teachings of the Buddha-dharma, can cause them to embrace all-knowledge (sarvajñajñāna) and also cause them to maintain all-knowledge.”

It causes one to embrace all-knowledge (sarvajñajñāna) and also causes one to sustain all-knowledge; that is to say, it bestows the sublime merit of Arhats and other beings, immeasurable and boundless.

In this way, when a bodhisattva wishes to realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, they are able to provide instruction and counsel through the perfections of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom, as well as other immeasurable and boundless Buddha-dharmas; thus, they provide instruction and counsel to immeasurable and boundless sentient beings, leading them to practice various kinds of peaceful and wondrous deeds.
In this way, a bodhisattva dwelling in the perfection of ethical discipline reflects:
"By virtue of my abiding in the bodhisattva perfection of ethical discipline, may all sentient beings be endowed with pure ethical discipline and remain far removed from its transgression."

"By means of these roots of goodness dedicated through such transference, may all sentient beings attain right mindfulness, and by virtue of that right mindfulness, may they all give rise to joy and happiness.
When those sentient beings heard these words, their minds were freed from transgressions, and they undertook the observance of pure precepts.

Furthermore, there is a bodhisattva who, dwelling securely in the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīlapāramitā*), gives with a single-minded resolve the ethical discipline in which they abide to a single bodhisattva; this surpasses the aforementioned merit by a hundredfold, a thousandfold, and even by a *upaniṣad*-fold.

In this way, whenever a bodhisattva, for the sake of sentient beings, dedicates the precepts they observe to other bodhisattvas, at those very times the bodhisattva’s perfection of ethical discipline gradually increases, and they are swiftly able to realize the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna).

“In this way, when a bodhisattva dwells securely in the perfection of ethical discipline, the various distinctions of the mass of merit obtained through dedicating it to sentient beings [are inconceivable].
At that time, Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!...”
How should such a bodhisattva be known? Through how many kalpas should such a bodhisattva be expected to attain liberation?
How long has it been since such a bodhisattva set out upon the Great Vehicle?
At that time, the Buddha addressed Śāriputra, saying:

“It should be known that such bodhisattvas are able to instruct and admonish all sentient beings through the perfections of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom, causing them to resolve upon unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment, to practice the various bodhisattva deeds without error, and to swiftly realize unexcelled, perfect, and complete awakening, thereby bringing great benefit to all sentient beings.”

It should be understood that such a bodhisattva, by means of the perfections of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom, dedicates these for the sake of all sentient beings with the aspiration to attain the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna), thinking thus:
"May I dedicate this perfection of generosity that I have practiced to all sentient beings, so that those who are stingy and greedy may all be able to practice generosity;
may I dedicate this perfection of ethical discipline that I have practiced to all sentient beings, so that those who violate ethical discipline may all attain pure ethical discipline."
May I dedicate this cultivation of the perfection of patience to all sentient beings, so that those who harbor anger and resentment may all attain patience;
may I dedicate this cultivation of the perfection of diligence to all sentient beings, so that those who are indolent may all attain diligence;
may I dedicate this cultivation of the perfection of meditative concentration to all sentient beings, so that those with distracted minds may all attain meditative concentration.
“May I dedicate this practice of the *prajñāpāramitā* to all sentient beings, so that those with impaired wisdom may all attain sublime wisdom.
At that time, Śāriputra again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“If a bodhisattva thus dedicates their own roots of goodness to the class of sentient beings, through how many eons must they practice the Mahāyāna before they can achieve liberation?”
At that time, the Buddha addressed Śāriputra, saying:
“In this way, when a bodhisattva dedicates their own roots of virtue to sentient beings and practices the Mahāyāna for five hundred great eons, they shall attain liberation.”
"Furthermore, Śāriputra!
There may be bodhisattvas who have accomplished skillful means and wish to swiftly realize the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna);
they shall, within this very Bhadrakalpa, vow to become Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas, and, being counted among the thousand Buddhas, realize unexcelled, perfect enlightenment."

Just as the Buddha Maitreya will empty all the evil realms and, at his first assembly, bring hundreds of thousands of koṭis of śrāvakas to the realization of arhatship through his teaching of the Dharma;

so too, I declare that this bodhisattva has already cultivated the practices for enlightenment for two thousand kalpas, seeking to realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening, desiring to bring great benefit to sentient beings.

If other bodhisattvas possess the aforementioned practices, characteristics, and signs, it should be known that they will attain liberation after training in the Mahāyāna for five hundred great kalpas; such bodhisattvas should be known as already dwelling in the stage of non-retrogression.
Then, Śāriputra again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“If bodhisattvas hear such teachings on the dharmas associated with these pāramitās, they should give rise to joy.”

Why is this? If bodhisattvas, upon hearing such teachings on the dharmas associated with these pāramitās, give rise to joy, they will certainly not abandon the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, and the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, will likewise not abandon them.
At that time, the Buddha addressed Śāriputra, saying: "So it is! So it is!"
It is as you have said.

If bodhisattvas, upon hearing such teachings on the dharmas associated with these perfections (*pāramitā*), remain for one full day and night with their hearts filled with continuous and profound joy, it should be known that these bodhisattvas have long since set out upon the Great Vehicle (*mahāyāna*).

If bodhisattvas, upon hearing such teachings on the dharmas associated with these perfections, remain for two full days and nights with their hearts filled with continuous and profound joy, it should be known that these bodhisattvas have likewise long since set out upon the Great Vehicle.

If bodhisattvas, upon hearing such teachings on the dharmas associated with the pāramitās, maintain a state of deep-seated joy continuously for three days and nights, or even up to seven days and nights, it should be known that these bodhisattvas have set out in the Mahāyāna for a long time, even for a very long time.
Then, Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:

"As I understand the meaning of what the Buddha has taught, these bodhisattvas who have set out in the Great Vehicle have already passed through one hundred eons, or two hundred eons, or three hundred eons, and so on, up to seven hundred eons."
These bodhisattvas, practicing the Mahāyāna, shall attain liberation after seven hundred kalpas.
By virtue of these causes and conditions, their merit and roots of goodness will gradually increase.
These bodhisattvas, through their skillful means, hear such teachings on the dharmas associated with the pāramitās; although they feel profound joy, they remain free from attachment.
"These bodhisattvas are pure by their very nature; upon hearing the teaching of the Mahāyāna, they rejoice with profound resolve.
At that time, the Buddha addressed Śāriputra, saying: "It is so! It is so!"
So it is! It is just as you have said.
By relying on the power of the Buddha, you are able to proclaim such teachings on the dharmas corresponding to the pāramitās.

If the assembly of bodhisattva mahāsattvas possesses the practices, characteristics, and signs as previously described, it should be known that they have long since set out upon the Great Vehicle; such bodhisattva mahāsattvas have already become non-retrogressive regarding the mind of enlightenment (bodhicitta).
If bodhisattvas do not give rise to joy upon hearing such teachings on the dharmas associated with these pāramitās, it should be known that these bodhisattvas have not long set out in the Mahāyāna.

For these bodhisattvas who have newly entered the Mahāyāna, I shall likewise proclaim the teachings corresponding to the pāramitās, so that by diligently practicing and training in them, they may gradually realize the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna).
At that time, Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
How extraordinary!"
“The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha does not abandon any bodhisattvas.
At that time, the Buddha said to Śāriputra:
“Do you think that the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha only does not abandon the bodhisattvas?”
You should not now hold such a view. Why is this? Śāriputra!

All Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas never abandon any sentient being; all Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas deeply compassionately regard all sentient beings, constantly forming this thought regarding them:
"By what skillful means can I cause those sentient beings to swiftly attain liberation from the suffering of saṃsāra?"
"Furthermore, Śāriputra! You should know that the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, possess minds of equanimity.

Just as they give rise to a pure and sincere mind toward a Buddha—abiding in compassion and loving-kindness, wishing to bestow happiness and remove suffering—they likewise regard all sentient beings with such pity, desiring equally to cause them to be free from suffering and to attain happiness."
"Furthermore, Śāriputra!
If the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas were to dwell with a distinct mind toward all Buddhas,
with a distinct mind toward all Bodhisattvas, with a distinct mind toward all Pratyekabuddhas, and toward the [Śrāvakas]..."
The Arhat dwells with a distinct mind; he dwells with a distinct mind toward the Non-returner, with a distinct mind toward the Once-returner,
with a distinct mind toward the Stream-enterer, with a distinct mind toward the Dharma-follower,
with a distinct mind toward the Faith-follower, and with a distinct mind toward those possessing the five external supernatural powers.
If one dwells with a distinct mind toward those who have attained the Prātimokṣa precepts,
with a distinct mind toward those who have accomplished the ten paths of wholesome action, with a distinct mind toward those who have committed the ten paths of unwholesome action,
and with a distinct mind toward Caṇḍālas, Pukkasas, and the like, then [the Tathāgatas, Arhats...]
If the mind of a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha were subject to differentiation and acted according to desire,
he would not be a Tathāgata,
Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha. Furthermore, Śāriputra!

However, the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas, just as they give rise to a pure mind toward a Buddha—abiding in compassion and the wish to bestow happiness and remove suffering—they do exactly the same toward a Bodhisattva.
Just as one gives rise to a pure mind toward a bodhisattva, abiding in compassion and the desire to bestow happiness and remove suffering, so too does one do so toward a pratyekabuddha.
Just as one gives rise to a pure mind toward a pratyekabuddha, abiding in compassion and the desire to bestow happiness and remove suffering, so too does one do so toward an arhat.
Just as one gives rise to a pure mind toward an Arhat, abiding in compassion and the desire to bestow happiness and remove suffering, so it is likewise toward a Non-returner (Anāgāmin).
Just as one gives rise to a pure mind toward a Non-returner, abiding in compassion and the desire to bestow happiness and remove suffering, so it is likewise toward a Once-returner (Sakṛdāgāmin).
Just as one gives rise to a pure mind toward a once-returner, abiding in compassion and the wish to bestow happiness and remove suffering, so too does one do so toward a stream-enterer.

Just as one gives rise to a pure mind toward a stream-enterer, abiding in compassion and the wish to bestow happiness and remove suffering, so too does one do so toward one who practices in accordance with the Dharma.

Just as one gives rise to a pure mind toward those who practice in accordance with the Dharma (dharmānusārin), abiding in compassion and the desire to bestow happiness and remove suffering, so too is it with those who practice in accordance with faith (śraddhānusārin).

Just as one gives rise to a pure mind toward those who practice in accordance with faith, abiding in compassion and the desire to bestow happiness and remove suffering, so too is it with the five external supernormal powers (pañcābhijñā).

Just as one gives rise to a pure mind toward the five external supernormal powers, abiding in compassion and the desire to bestow happiness and remove suffering, so too is it with respect to all attainments of the Pratimokṣa vows.

Just as one gives rise to a pure mind toward those who have accomplished the prātimokṣa precepts, dwelling in compassion and the desire to bestow happiness and remove suffering, so too should one act toward all who have accomplished the ten paths of wholesome action.

Just as one gives rise to a pure mind toward those who have accomplished the ten paths of wholesome action, abiding in compassion and the desire to bring them happiness and remove their suffering, so too should one do for those who have accomplished the ten paths of unwholesome action.

Just as one gives rise to a pure mind toward those who have accomplished the ten paths of unwholesome action, dwelling in compassion and the desire to bring them happiness and remove their suffering, one should do likewise even for those such as the Caṇḍālas and Pukkasas.
Because the mind of a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha is without differentiation and does not act according to desire, he is called a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha.
Therefore, the Buddhas, endowed with great compassion and wisdom, abide in the state of equality regarding all phenomena and never abandon any sentient being.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!

I do not see any Buddha, World-Honored One, giving rise to attachment or aversion toward objects of perception or even toward minor matters; it is impossible for any Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha to give rise to attachment, aversion, or the like regarding objects of perception.
Why is this? Śāriputra, it is because the Buddhas,
the World-Honored Ones, have forever severed all afflictions, such as attachment and aversion.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra!
All Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas never abandon Bodhisattvas. Why is this?

Śāriputra! After the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas, there are bodhisattvas who, through diligent practice, gradually fulfill the pāramitās of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom;

and who, through ardent study, gradually fulfill the non-perverted wisdom regarding internal emptiness, external emptiness, internal-and-external emptiness, the emptiness of emptiness, great emptiness, ultimate emptiness, conditioned emptiness, unconditioned emptiness, absolute emptiness, boundless emptiness, dispersed emptiness, non-altering emptiness, essential emptiness, self-characteristic emptiness, common-characteristic emptiness, the emptiness of all phenomena, the emptiness of non-apprehensibility, the emptiness of non-existence, the emptiness of intrinsic nature, and the emptiness of the non-existence of intrinsic nature.

Through diligent cultivation and study, he gradually perfects non-erroneous wisdom regarding the true suchness (*tathatā*) of all phenomena, the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*), the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), their non-falsity, their immutability, their equality, their freedom from birth, the fixed order of phenomena (*dharmaniyāmatā*), the stability of phenomena (*dharmaniyāmatā*), the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), the realm of space (*ākāśadhātu*), and the inconceivable realm;

and through diligent cultivation and study, he gradually perfects non-erroneous wisdom regarding the dependent origination of formations conditioned by ignorance, consciousness conditioned by formations, name-and-form conditioned by consciousness, the six sense bases conditioned by name-and-form, contact conditioned by the six sense bases, feeling conditioned by contact, craving conditioned by feeling, grasping conditioned by craving, existence conditioned by grasping, birth conditioned by existence, and old age and death conditioned by birth.

Through diligent cultivation and study, because ignorance ceases, volitional formations cease; because volitional formations cease, consciousness ceases; because consciousness ceases, name-and-form cease; because name-and-form cease, the six sense bases cease; because the six sense bases cease, contact ceases; because contact ceases, feeling ceases; because feeling ceases, craving ceases; because craving ceases, clinging ceases; because clinging ceases, existence ceases; because existence ceases, birth ceases; and because birth ceases, old age and death cease. Thus, non-perverted wisdom is gradually perfected.
Through diligent cultivation and study, non-perverted wisdom regarding the Noble Truths of suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path is gradually perfected.
Through diligent cultivation and study, the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless attainments are gradually perfected.

Through diligent cultivation and study, they gradually bring to full completion the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path;
through diligent cultivation and study, they gradually bring to full completion the gateways to liberation of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness;

and through diligent cultivation and study, they gradually bring to full completion the eight liberations, the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive meditative attainments, and the ten totalities.

Through diligent cultivation and study, they gradually perfect the non-erroneous wisdom of the stages of the Pure Contemplation, the Lineage, the Eighth, the Possession of Vision, the Thinness, the Freedom from Desire, the Accomplishment, the Pratyekabuddha, the Bodhisattva, and the Tathāgata;

After the parinirvāṇa of all Tathāgatas, there will be bodhisattva-mahāsattvas in the worlds of the ten directions who realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening, acting as illuminators for all the worlds.

It is like a great tree with many fruits and leaves; after it has withered and perished, a small tree grows up in its place. Its trunk, stem, branches, and twigs gradually grow taller and wider, casting a canopy of shade for one *yojana* in circumference. Countless sentient beings take shelter beneath it, escaping hardships such as wind, rain, cold, and heat, and they gather and enjoy its fruits and leaves. All wise people praise it in unison.

In this way, the fruits, leaves, and shade of this great tree continue to benefit and bring joy to sentient beings no differently than in the past; it is only the foolish who do not understand how to rely upon them.

Likewise, after the Parinirvāṇa of the Buddha, the World-Honored One, these Bodhisattvas gradually train in and perfect the pāramitās of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom, as well as the other boundless sublime dharmas of the Buddhas. They successively attain unexcelled, perfect enlightenment in each of the trichiliocosm worlds, succeeding the former Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas, to truly benefit and gladden immeasurable sentient beings and ensure that the various Buddha-activities are never interrupted.

That is to say, for the sake of infinite sentient beings, he skillfully expounds various Dharma gates—such as the ten paths of wholesome action, generosity, ethical discipline, and cultivation—urging them to practice diligently so that they may escape the suffering of the evil realms and be born among gods and humans to experience all manner of happiness.

For the sake of infinite sentient beings, he employs skillful means to proclaim the aggregates, bases, and elements, as well as the absence of a self, a sentient being, a life-force, a soul, a nourisher, a person, an individual, a mind-born, a youth, an agent, an experiencer, a knower, or a viewer. He causes them to apply themselves with diligence to the correct contemplation of the four noble truths—suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path—and to cultivate the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, the eightfold noble path, the three doors of liberation, and other wholesome dharmas, thereby severing all afflictions and attaining parinirvāṇa.

"By means of skillful methods, they proclaim such immeasurable categories of Dharma-gates to inspire diligent effort; by means of skillful means, they skillfully and non-erroneously contemplate, remaining free from all conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*); and by means of skillful means, they practice the perfections of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom, as well as other immeasurable and boundless Buddha-dharmas, until they ultimately realize the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*)."

Among all classes of sentient beings, those who possess discerning wisdom, upon hearing such a Dharma, practice it with diligence; according to their respective capacities, they attain the flavor of the Deathless (amṛta), receiving temporary or ultimate benefit and peace. Only the ignorant followers of external paths (tīrthika) are unable to hear and accept it, remaining submerged and wandering through the various realms of existence.

At that time, Śāriputra again addressed the Buddha, saying:

"As I understand the meaning of what the Buddha has taught, even if one were to instruct and teach hundreds, thousands, or even countless persons of the Śrāvaka vehicle, causing them all to dwell securely in the fruit of Arhatship, it would not equal teaching the essential points of the profound Dharma through skillful means to a single person of the Bodhisattva vehicle—namely, the teachings corresponding to the six *pāramitās*—so that upon hearing them, they might give rise to a single thought-moment associated with omniscience (*sarvajñatā*)."

Such essential teachings are the most supreme, the most excellent, the most venerable, the most exalted, the most sublime, the most subtle, the highest, and the unsurpassed among all previous teachings, because the mind thus generated is the most superior among all the merits of the śrāvakas and others.
At that time, the Buddha praised Śāriputra, saying:
"Excellent! Excellent!"
It is as you have said.

You are able to act as a true disciple of the Buddha; being wise, discerning, well-disciplined, and fearless, you shall instruct and guide those who follow the Bodhisattva vehicle, causing them to diligently practice the various bodhisattva deeds so that they may swiftly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, thereby bringing great benefit to all sentient beings.
At that time, the Buddha addressed Ānanda, saying:
"You should receive and uphold the perfection of pure ethical discipline cultivated by the assembly of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas as spoken by Śāriputra; do not let it be forgotten or lost!"
Ānanda said: “So be it, World-Honored One!”
I have already received and upheld the perfection of pure ethical discipline as practiced by the assembly of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, as taught by Śāriputra; I shall certainly never forget it!
May those bodhisattvas who have not yet resolved upon unsurpassed bodhicitta quickly resolve their minds upon it;
may those who have already resolved upon unsurpassed bodhicitta never again fall back;

and for those who have already reached the stage of non-retrogression regarding unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, may they swiftly bring the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna) to full perfection.

When the Blessed One had spoken this sutra, the Venerable Śāriputra, the Venerable Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra, the Venerable Ānanda, and the rest of the assembly of śrāvakas and bodhisattvas, as well as all others—devas, nāgas, yakṣas, humans, non-humans, and so forth—hearing what the Buddha had taught, were all greatly rejoiced, and they faithfully accepted and practiced it.
